newsitem.title: CHINA: Hongkong Bank sees calmer H2 after mortgage war.
newsitem.headline: Hongkong Bank sees calmer H2 after mortgage war.

text.p: HSBC Holdings Plc unit Hongkong Bank Group said it experienced intense competition in the residential mortgage market in the first half of 1997 but saw a "calmer" second half.
"We think we are entering a slightly calmer period," HSBC Holdings Plc chief executive John Bond said in Hong Kong on Monday.

The Hongkong Bank Group, the chief Asian entity of HSBC Holdings, maintained its market share in most sectors, but saw intense competition in the residential mortgage market in Hong Kong in the first six months of the year, executives said.
Margins on mortgages were squeezed and the resulting decline in profitability was only partially offset by the large increase in the volume of lending, the bank's results statements showed.

The Hongkong Bank Group announced profit attributable to shareholders of HK$10.31 billion, a 6.7 percent increase over the year-earlier period. Operating profit before provisions rose 14.1 percent to HK$14.91 billion.
The slower rate of growth at the attributable profit level was due chiefly to the fall in profits on the disposals of assets, Bond said.
The profit on disposal of fixed assets and investment securities was HK$573 million, significantly lower than the HK$1.23 billion reported in the first half of 1996, the statement said.
The rate of earnings growth was also held back by a dealing loss of about 40 million sterling in equities underwriting by the investment bank, Bond said.
"Our business in Hong Kong made good progress although we experienced continuing pressure on spreads," Hongkong Bank Group chairman John Strickland said.
"Advances to customers grew strongly. Demand for residential mortgages was high, but we remain comfortable with our overall exposure to the property market," Strickland said

Total advances to customers increased by 17 percent, boosted by a 23 percent rise in advances in Hongkong Bank in Hong Kong and by an 18 percent rise in advances by 61-percent owned subsidiary Hang Seng Bank Ltd, the results statement said.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, has been keeping a close watch on banks' property-related lending, but said it did not yet see the need to further restrict banks' lending.

In a letter to banks dated July 28, the authority said banks' whose property exposure was above the overall industry average of about 40 percent of loans should be attempting to stabilise or reduce that percentage.
The Hongkong Bank's exposure to property was about 40 percent of the loan portfolio, Strickland said in March 1997.
The bank group's net interest margin fell to 2.79 percent from 2.87 percent and the return on average shareholders' funds slipped to 24.2 percent from 27.5 percent.
Hang Seng Bank reported a 14.5 percent rise in attributable profit to HK$4.98 billion in the first half.
"We remain positive about the outlook for the region, notwithstanding the recent volatility in some Asian currencies," said Strickland.

In first half 1997, Hongkong Bank achieved significant growth in operating profit before provisions in other areas in Asia, particularly Australia, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand and New Zealand, the statement said.
Operating profit before provisions in India and Korea fell in difficult markets, it said.
Reportingly separately, Hongkong Bank Malaysia Bhd reported a 14.5 percent rise in profit after tax to 179.4 million ringgit.
